121.t: A Girl from Cucamonga and the Double Whammy dispute
121.s: Who decided what was recorded; Girl from Cucamonga as an Oop-Oop-A-Doo takeoff, and Freddie King's chart hit with Double Whammy that Ridgley plans to pursue through an attorney.
121.q: No. No. Joe had, yeah. Joe had. But how it was, we recorded the tunes that we thought were good. We did more. We did more like that. She just liked it because a girl from Cucamonga. That was a take off on Oop Oop Adu. Yeah. And Oop Oop Adu was a big tune and so I don't know, I just wrote the girl…

121.t: Tudor Square and half the publishing on Sometime You Get It
121.s: Ridgley recorded for Sansu, the station dropped it for lack of money, and Marshall agreed to give half the publishing so Ridgley could release it on Tudor Square.
121.q: Yeah. I did this with C-Saint. Sometime you get it and sometime you don't. And what happened, we had a thing going when the station over right over there. Clyde L. Yeah. Well, whatever station was, we had it. We had it going pretty good. And they put this on. They put the on program. And one of the…

121.t: Ruffino's two sets of books and how many records Ridgley made
121.s: Ruffino paid small sums, no royalty statements and kept two sets of books; records kept Ridgley's name alive, perhaps in the 50s counted.
121.q: They kept me working. You know what? They kept my name flourishing quite a bit. And you see, I'm looking at that. That's quite a few records.

121.t: Double Eye Whammy and Freddie King's San Jose
121.s: Freddie King took his Rick record home and recorded San Jose, a hit, and later a vocal Double Eye Whammy, without payment.
121.q: Freddie King came down here, and he was on the cause. He was living on the causeway at Marino's Motel, and he and I got to be buddy buddies for a while. He was here because his cause broke down.

121.t: Recording in New York and the Griffin Brothers cover
121.s: In New York he wrote out lyrics and recorded a demo, the Griffin Brothers cover came out, and a salesman later said money was paid off.
121.ch: Tra La La and the Griffin Brothers
121.q: But anyway, and I look at it, and I remember how this thing went down. Now, what happened later on, I said about four or five years after that, they had this white belt. He was a sailman at Patterson Pontiac on Galveston Canal. I went in there. And my cousin was buying a car, a 1956 Pontiac. And so…

121.t: Sound of New Orleans and Gary Edwards: no pay
121.s: Saints-themed songs by Janice Medlow recorded for Gary Edwards; Ridgley never got paid though musicians and Wardell were.
121.q: Sound of New Orleans. Gary, Gary Edwards. Gary Edwards. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. This, these tunes, these tunes were done, uh, uh, what her name, Medlow. This, this lady, she, she, she, she, she, she, she's working in the hotels downtown now. Uh-huh. Janice Medlow. Okay,…

30.t: Bechet selling tunes and why he left Duke
30.s: Bechet could earn more without Duke and, like Bigard, sold tunes for $25 or $50, some to Duke and Irving Mills; Bigard says Bechet could not get along with anybody.
30.q: No. He could make more money without Duke. You see, Bechet wrote a lot of tunes, you know, and he would sell them just like we all did at the time. $25, $50. You know, it was kind of nice money for them to drink especially. Like I sold Mood Indigo for $25. That's, you know --

30.t: Getting Kid Ory his Muskrat Ramble royalties
30.s: Learning Ory never saw royalties, Bigard traced the song from Melrose to publisher John Levy, who gave Ory a check for about $8,500, then $700 each quarter; Bigard says Ellington and Mills had tricked him.
30.q: So he did that. In the meantime Bob Crosby was playing his tune 'Muskrat Ramble' all the time, you know, and he wrote it. So I asked him one day, I says, "Hey, 'Dud,' isn't that your tune?" He said, "Yes." I said, "Are you getting any royalties?" He said, "No." I said, "Well, who published it?" He…

30.t: Why Bigard cannot recover back royalties on 'Mood Indigo'
30.s: Willard asks why there is no retroactive money; Bigard says Mills and Ellington were already paid, that his name was missing for 28 years, and that he has thirteen tunes there.
30.q: Uh-uh. And there's 20 years of it, too. 28 years. Can you imagine that? I wrote 13 tunes I got in there. Now I got -- I just wrote five tunes now. They're coming out on this record.

30.t: How his name reached 'Mood Indigo' and the ASCAP three-hit rule
30.s: His name got onto 'Mood Indigo' after the 28th year when it was reissued; ASCAP required three hits for membership until BMI began buying numbers.
30.q: After the 28th year when they re-issued it. Can you imagine that? And that was the time, you see, when to belong to ASCAP you had to write at least three hits. You see, that's where the mess-up come, because you couldn't belong to ASCAP if you didn't write three hits.

30.t: Publishers shelving tunes and then releasing them under their own names
30.s: Publishers asked for submissions, put them on the shelf for years and then published them under the company's name, so people now publish their own music.
30.q: do? I mean, they -- like you take a -- say, for instance, you write a tune and you send it to Mills, Berlin, or any publishing house and you tell them -- like they're always saying, "Send in a tune," you know, and you send it to them and tell them to look it over.

30.t: 'Crawfish Blues' royalties of 49 cents and the unfinished Pelican Trio record
30.s: His blues with Zutty, called 'Crawfish Blues', earned him 49 cents after sixteen years from Mickey Goldsen, and the last Pelican Trio session got hung up and is unfinished.
30.q: When I recorded with Zutty and made a blues, he called it the 'Crawfish Blues.' He called it the 'Crawfish Blues.' So I get a big royalty on that -- 75 cents every three months, --

124.t: McRae's staff-writer contract with Robbins Music
124.s: The Robbins deal was an advance against royalties of a thousand dollars, rising to five and ten thousand yearly.
124.ch: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
124.q: This was to (inaudible) cover any amount of songs. Just was an advance of a thousand dollars. You know, (inaudible) in the 40's -- In those days, somebody give you a thousand dollars, that was a lot of money. You're talking about in the 40's and the 30's. 40's now, right? Nobody was passing a --

124.t: Royalties and writing "Back Bay Shuffle" for Artie Shaw
124.s: The song sold well abroad; Shaw and McRae both signed with Robbins and agreed to split credit on songs written for him.
124.ch: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
124.q: I did "Back Bay" for Artie and "Traffic Jam" for Artie. They were also Jack Robbins tunes too. Artie was signed to Robbins Music and I was signed to Robbins Music.

124.t: Artie Shaw gives up his band; unrecorded tunes
124.s: Robbins told McRae he lost half a million dollars when Shaw quit, leaving unrecorded McRae tunes.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: And then he decided he wanted to go -- you know, be an author. He wanted to write books. Jack Robbins called me up one day and say, "Look, you just lost a half a million dollars." I say, "Why?" "Your favorite boy just give up his band, Artie Shaw."

124.t: Joining ASCAP and publishing through Robbins
124.s: Before 1945 McRae's songs sat with Robbins Music; joining ASCAP with a whole catalog let him collect back revenue.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: All our things were in Robbins Music, you know. See, when I was writing for Artie, Artie was a arranger and he had signed with Robbins Music for all his music -- it went into Robbins. Everything like -- Way before I joined Artie -- remember the little band he had? You know, he was writing -- he put…

124.t: Mistaken credit for Joe Thomas's song in a film
124.s: Shapiro-Bernstein thought a song used by Glenn Miller and Artie Shaw was McRae's, but it belonged to the other tenor player named Joe Thomas.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: No. Not -- he called me one day and thought they had 'Back Bay Shuffle' or one of the things (inaudible) Glen Gray had did, but it wasn't mine. It was the other tenor player. Remember the tenor player who had the band with Louie before I took the band over? I think his name was Joe Thomas, too. He…

124.t: Sally Webb and copyright renewals through John Eastman
124.s: McRae put Chick Webb's widow in touch with lawyer John Eastman, who paid for the renewals of Chick's copyrights.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: Moe Gale had to give her the money. Now on top of that, all these things were going on -- See, just because I left the band, it was a lot of other things that had to be -- I had to do before I finished out that area with Ella. It was an area where Sally, his wife -- she was living up in Jersey --…

10.t: Froggy Moore Blues credit dispute with Melrose and Hafer
10.s: Carew objects to a record crediting Seitz, Oliver and Melrose on Morton's tune, blaming Melrose and a Hafer note, and the license he gave Melrose.
10.q: Yes, well I have a recording that he made of Froggy Moore, and they called it Froggy Moore Blues. I don't know, I'm not sweating about that yet. They called it Froggy Moore Blues, and on the outside of the cover, it says this tune, the King Oliver tune, Froggy Moore's blues, so and so and so, went…

10.t: Local publishers and publishing The Full Moon Rag in 1909
10.s: Carew recalls Williams and Pirone, other New Orleans publishers, and getting The Full Moon Rag published by Pewter in 1909.
10.q: close to that is that at the corner Canal and Rampart Street there used to be a small open truck, one of these light delivery trucks with an open wagon. And they had a couple of pieces of music in that, and a Negro standing in the back or sitting in the back singing. They used to give a little…

10.t: Froggy Moore, Spikes Brothers and the title's meaning
10.s: Carew explains how Morton's Froggy Moore was split and republished, and debates whether the title refers to a contortionist or Freddie Moore.
10.q: Well, he, uh, he wrote Frogger. He wrote Froggy Moore. Then he went out west, uh, uh, at least he was in Los Angeles, and, uh, he played it for Spice Brothers, and got hooked up with them, and they, they took part one and part three and wrote, uh, Froggy Moore. Mm-hmm. See? Just used those two…

10.t: Publishing more Morton pieces after his death and Lomax's book
10.s: After Morton died, Lomax asked to quote tunes, and Carew published Mamie's Blues, Buddy Bolden's Blues and others.
10.q: yes and we probably we published five pieces while he was alive there we published that we are elks yes and that was the last one then he died and uh along comes lomax about 19 well i don't know what but anyway whenever he probably was probably getting his book published he asked me to permit him…

10.t: Tempo Music Publishing, Clarence Williams and sales of the songs
10.s: They discuss the company name, using Clarence Williams as agent, print runs, sales of 300 to 500, and bands borrowing the music.
10.ch: Jelly Roll Morton and Tempo Music
10.q: song we decided on the name of the company tempo music publishing company i suggested that he says that's okay so i used that name and sent him up to new york to look up a publisher after we got the manuscripts in form and he went up there and he asked clarence williams he says i think i can get…

234.t: Record companies want half the publishing
234.s: Gil says companies demand half the publishing rights, and Johnston compares it to earlier cases of Black composers being cheated.
234.ch: Japan trip, publishing and early influences
234.q: Even with the composers. A lot of times a record company wont release your music unless you give them half the publishing. That happens now. I took my tapes the other day, I have two tapes, a USA and a Japanese tape that I wanted to play for you (on Sunday?). And this man said he liked them very…

234.t: The publisher made him buy his own score
234.s: Gil says a publisher would not give him a complimentary copy of the score to his album.
234.ch: Japan trip, publishing and early influences
234.q: The publisher made me go out and buy the score. He wouldn't give me a complimentary copy of that music until after this album which put

234.t: Stories of Black musicians losing their recordings and songs
234.s: Johnston and Gil trade stories of demo records issued commercially without pay, and Gil says exploitation crosses color lines.
234.q: Well people do that to each other regardless of race, color or creed. (LAUGHTER). I mean white black people do that to each other and black people do that to each other. I mean I know one black man who bought, (one man who bought another ones composition reputedly for for, twenty five dollars and…

234.t: Copyright suits: Chuck Berry, the Beatles and the Beach Boys
234.s: Gil tells of a lawyer winning money for Chuck Berry from the Beatles' publisher and suggests suing the Beach Boys.
234.q: Oh, they got more than that, but it took three years to get it. And also it was from the Beatles. Because you know the Beatles had been ripping him off a lot. But they like him so much and everything so they came to the hearing to court, /and said yes, they, they wanted him to win. In other words,…

234.t: 'Light My Fire' claims and being copied without a fee
234.s: Gil describes a Columbia man urging him to sue over 'Light My Fire', and a film composer who used his record without paying.
234.q: : So I mean in cases like that you can institute a suit. It ~~es~~ takeSa long time. Somebody wanted me to do that for a tune I wrote that they said that the Doors ~~M~~ copied, 'Lite My Fire'. 'Lite My Fire' was such a big hit and sold to Buick and all that. So the man at Columbia was, caught on…

18.s: He has collected royalties since 1929 on his own tunes and explains how leaders took credit in the past.
18.ch: Russell and Armstrong years, Goodman and the road
18.q: From Higginbotham Blues, Give Me Your Telephone Number and a guy will call me up and say ... and there's some other tunes. I don't know. played the record the other day swing out,

18.s: Irene wrote a song for him; she belonged to ASCAP while he never filled in the form; he collects royalties since 1929.
18.q: I said I should be, but I didn't do that. I just didn't do it, period. ... They gave me a slip to fill out and I didn't do it...

18.t: Irving Mills's name on songs and credit for Ride Red Ride
18.s: Publisher Irving Mills put his name on tunes in exchange for recording; JCH was uncredited on Ride Red Ride.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: He's a big publisher. I got his name on a record back there. I haven't been paid for it, haven't collected for it. I will if I take time. Any record you record, just like when I was with Lucky Millinder's band, if you want to make a record you write a tune. This is your tune. So the leader says,…

18.t: The trombone solo book and Leeds buying music
18.s: His small trombone solo book is published by Mills; Leeds was buying up black and white music in the late 1930s.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: Yes. There's a book - you saw the trombone book in there.

18.s: Scale was about $50 for four sides of three minutes fifteen; the band knew the tunes from nightly playing.
18.ch: Cincinnati, Buffalo, Russell and Fletcher Henderson
18.q: I don't know how many times. Of course, see, we knew practically all the tunes ... because we were playing on a steady job and we used to play them practically every night.

77.t: Jobs without records; no royalties, reclaiming songs from MCA
77.s: In those days a record was not needed to get work; she was never paid royalties or session fees and hopes to get songs back under the new copyright law.
77.q: Yeah, you have to have a record now, that's really selling, in order to get work. But I was lucky enough to always go from one job to another without a record.

77.t: Paramount payments, Mayo Williams and Mr. Supper, royalties
77.s: M. A. Supper paid honestly while J. Mayo Williams was a thief; she got $75 a side and a quarter-cent royalty, and only got her copyright back from Mills.
77.ch: Records, Lovie Austin and a first marriage
77.q: He was the -- I think he's the one that first came into Dreamland and spoke to me about recording. But Mr. Supper, Mr. M. A. Supper, the white fellow -- J. Mayo Williams was a colored man, Negro man. Mr. Supper was a white man and a very fine, honest man.

77.t: MCA's offer to renew a copyright and signing away rights
77.s: MCA recently asked her to sign away all rights to "You've Got to Reap What You Sow"; she showed it to a lawyer at AGAC and renews her own copyrights.
77.ch: New Orleans musicians, recordings and radio
77.q: Anyhow, I had a letter from him. At first the young man called me and said that they wanted to go -- they were going to renew You've Got to Reap What You Sow. So -- and sent me a thing for me to sign. You sign away your -- all rights. How stupid do they --

77.t: Getting her song back from Bess Berman after Mahalia Jackson recorded it
77.s: Apollo's Bess Berman put out Mahalia's version of Hunter's song under a changed title; Mahalia announced the true author at a Brooklyn concert and Hunter got her song back.
77.q: Yeah. What's -- I got that record. I got some of those records too. What was her first one? You see, I wrote a song called, 'Will The Day Ever Come When I Can Rest,' and I took it down to Bess Berman, who owned the record company at the time.

77.t: Cheated by Mayo Williams but now paid foreign royalties
77.s: She got a few hundred dollars for the biggest record ever, but now receives "Downhearted Blues" royalties from Scandinavia and welcomes new law letting authors recall contracts.
77.ch: Gangsters, records, women musicians and the blues
77.q: I'm still getting money. But the contract, just think, I got a fourth of a penny. I was supposed to get a fourth of a penny on the record and I didn't get that. Isn't that unkind? You know, fate's a -- but I'm living to tell it. That's the part I'm proud of.

83.t: BMI versus ASCAP and Levy Music
83.s: Matassa's Pontchartrain was BMI while his Levy Music was ASCAP but unused; he explains ASCAP was an old writers' club hostile to upstarts and weighted payouts.
83.q: Because nobody crossed my path. Nobody crossed my path. Well, one lady. One lady. But, but I gave her her songs back when she moved out of town. Uh, she was a writer.

83.t: Art Rupe's hard bargains and the gospel group's advance
83.s: Rupe reported sales honestly but was miserly, adding a contract clause so a gospel group earned no royalties until an advance for a broken-down car was repaid.
83.q: Well, I have to qualify almost everybody. For instance, let's say Art Roop. Okay. One of the really big ones. I have no doubt in my mind, or I could be wrong, but I have no doubt in my mind that Art Roop reported sales correctly. Mm-hmm. That Art Roop was not a person who would sell X number of…

83.t: The Messner brothers, Syd Nathan and Jack Pearl
83.s: The Messners ran from a shoebox with nominal royalties and publishing grabs; King's Syd Nathan and lawyer Jack Pearl wrote harsh contracts.
83.q: Well, the Messners, oh, I think their arithmetic was bad. You know, I have no doubt that their arithmetic was bad. But I don't know, I have no way of proving it. Mm-hmm.

83.t: Cheap studio rates and the ease of entering the record business
83.s: Sessions cost $15 an hour, later $35, and living was cheap, so many small labels put out a record or two.
83.q: late 40s early 50s late 40s early 50s into the late 50s you know what your rates didn't didn't change didn't change much no when I got up to 35 dollars an hour I was in hog heaven um and and uh the cost of living was cheap down here you know yeah a guy could come down if he hung out with with the…

194.t: Atlantic contract terms and the sides released
194.s: Atlantic offered a hundred dollars plus session fee against royalties; he never saw royalties, and six sides were issued.
194.q: Well, he'd come up with a hundred dollars plus session fee, you know. Yeah. But, at that time that was plenty of money, you know, I guess.

194.s: He recorded four sides for King's Federal label; Joe Assunto handled business; he got session fees but no royalties.
194.q: I don't know, Joe Santo at that time was conducting the business part of the situation. Joe Santo was conducting the business.

194.t: Ballads and the second Mardi Gras record
194.s: He discusses his ballads and the later hit Mardi Gras in New Orleans, which still sells and on which he finally holds rights.
194.q: Yeah, I do some of the ballads today. I do the Cry Pretty Baby. The ballads were- The Cry Pretty Baby and Misery. I don't do that much anymore. Whenever you change his band you got to get the pieces to direct them to the changes and the measurements and the balls and all.

194.t: Botched first record, Mercury and Atlantic, and never getting paid
194.s: His first record was killed by a union problem, then he recorded for Mercury and Atlantic but received no statements or money and quit more than once.
194.q: I knew that was, that was the first thing I did on, on, uh, records, but, uh, I got it on. It didn't go to, I got it. Okay. It didn't go to. I don't think the fellas, it's, something happening that. He either wasn't a licensed, he either wasn't a licensed, uh, uh, operator, uh, he was out of his…

471.t: Eleana on sidemen's pay and the Helsinki tape
471.s: Eleana explains work for hire and how she got Cobb paid for a Coltrane tape.
471.ch: Kind of Blue business and anniversary tours
471.q: I would say starting around Kind of Blue, Jimmy – sidemen don’t get paid in this business. Just, they don’t. They do work for hire. Usually this record goes out there, they sell a few copies if they’re lucky. Sometimes – every once in a while, somebody like Herbie Hancock will get a hit tune, and…

471.t: Royalties, Sony and fairness to sidemen
471.s: Sidemen got nothing from the record's long sales, and Cobb hopes the union will help.
471.ch: Kind of Blue business and anniversary tours
471.q: But however – yeah, and then that’s according – they would charge him about how much it cost to produce a record. They would take that off of his share of the record. He’d be paying that a long time. Had he known that the record’s going to last 50 years, he would have really stuck them up, because…

471.t: Pay for Kind of Blue and the Wes Montgomery points
471.s: Cobb recalls the fee under $500, the release contract, and Miles suggesting he ask Wes for a point.
471.ch: Kind of Blue business and anniversary tours
471.q: I think back then a date was – what was it? I don’t know. It was a certain amount of money, but not a lot of money. I can’t even remember what it was, but it was under – I’m thinking it was under $500, way under $500. Then you have to sign some sort of agreement to even get that money. Then that…

471.t: The 40th anniversary and dealing with Sony
471.s: Eleana negotiated a one-time payment; Sony gave Cobb a snare drum.
471.ch: Kind of Blue business and anniversary tours
471.q: They approached us about doing some advertising for it, but even then they didn’t want – they think it’s gratis or something, that I’m supposed to do it because – I don’t know why they think I’m just supposed to do it because they say it. But they talked to my wife about doing it, and she says, “I…

80.t: Publishing 'Yacht Club Swing' and Fats adding his name
80.s: Jack Bregman published his tune in 1938; Fats put his name on it to help sales, and Autrey got a few dollars but not what he should have.
80.q: Well, I really -- maybe I shouldn't say the things I have said, because I don't have the proof. I was -- it was hearsay by some very important people. For instance, Bergaman? You remember him? Mr. Bergaman? Jack Bergaman? He's a publisher, vocal --

80.t: The publisher who bought a whole show to get one tune
80.s: Fats told him how Robbins bought a Broadway show that had gone to Paris just to obtain one tune and still made a quarter million.
80.q: Yes. Yes, because -- I'm trying to think of the publisher, because he was a little publisher himself, but the big guys had snowed him under, you know. He would say -- get to where he couldn't move. He couldn't -- you know. Because Fats told me the story about some man had a tune, and sold it to a…

80.t: Tunes made up on the club stand, and publishers copying them onto their cuffs
80.s: After hours at the club the band built tunes from Fats's chords while publishers like Archie Bleyer wrote them down and sold them back as stock arrangements.
80.q: No, not to -- no. No, not then. Not then. But I mean that did happen throughout the night. I mean after. Because when you're recording, or broadcasting, you want to be -- sound together. Want to be together, thinkingwise, playing. You know. Because you can't take too many shots in -- you don't know…

80.t: Feeling bad about being left behind, and why managers refuse unsolicited tunes
80.s: Fats told the band he left it to Kirkeby; Autrey explains how hearing thousands of submitted tunes leads to unconscious copying and suits.
80.q: Well I felt bad about it, but I didn't -- still didn't blame Fats, because I knew why, and Fats didn't do it. And Kirkoby did it. That's what I mean.

87.t: Missing royalties and his friendship with Mundy
87.s: His name was added later, after missing the first royalties; he says Billie Holiday's book reports $75 each, and he held no grudge against his friend.
87.ch: Virginia school and first Washington bands
87.q: Oh, well, I missed all of the royalties from the first record because my name wasn't on it then and -- from the first months of that Billie Holiday record. And that was the most lucrative part of it, you know. I got it all later, about a year or so later.

87.s: His tunes went into Lunceford and Oxley's publishing house, and he took it to an arbitration board for a little money.
87.q: some packed shows all day, you know. So -- but I know I had a problem. When I was writing tunes with Sy Oliver, we put a -- Lunceford had a publishing house called New Era Publishing House. He and Harold Oxley -- and we placed our tunes in his -- he was a publisher. They were publishers, and I know…

87.t: Timme Rosenkrantz's apartment recordings of Erroll Garner
87.s: A collector recorded Garner by the hour and later issued the records cheaply in Europe, undercutting Garner's sales.
87.ch: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
87.q: I don't know exactly what building that was, but -- it was -- recording was going on all over that place then, but they had a lot of good studios around there then, you know. The building might not have been much, but the recording facilities were good, you know, and Errol Garner was -- they had a…

87.s: A three-hour record date paid scale of $33, with no royalties though "Margie" sold in the millions.
87.q: Well, recordings in those days, what you got paid for -- a three hour record date in those days was $33.00, and that's it. Now, I made a record of "Margie" with Lunceford on a date, and I got $33.00 for the date, and the record was a big hit. It sold in the millions, this side, "Margie", but I…

17.t: Royalties, Love Records and the follow-up 'Topsy' recordings
17.s: Inexperienced backers botched the money; Cole recorded the follow-up LPs.
17.ch: Jamming, bootleg records and the Topsy hit
17.q: Oh yeah, yeah I got cheated out of some royalties, I'm so sorry that I couldn't make a hit record for a studio, an established, like a Decca or Victor or Brunswick or Columbia, somebody that was used to handling money. See, these kids weren't used to handling money and money was coming in too fast…

17.t: Bootleg recordings of jam sessions and concerts
17.s: Tapes of jam sessions and concerts get sold abroad; Cole recalls a manager ripping out hidden wires.
17.ch: Jamming, bootleg records and the Topsy hit
17.q: That's right, that's right, and no paid admission. But to go out there and sit in and jam where people are paying to come in that door, all they giving you is just a drink and a sandwich or a steak, whatever, you know, you got money, you can buy that. So you know and so those things I wouldn't…

17.t: 1930s session work: how dates were booked and what they paid
17.s: Leaders asked him at the club; three-hour sessions paid about $45-50.
17.ch: Stuff Smith, 52nd Street and session work
17.q: Mildred Bailey, Red Norvo, Joe Marsella, oh yeah, Red Norvo, Lionel, Ella, of course Sarah, Sarah Vaughn, the Andrews Sisters, yeah, I did a lot of recordings.

17.t: Cozy's Conception of Carmen on Everest without payment
17.s: Cole sees his MGM-era record reissued by Everest under a changed title and was never paid.
17.ch: Jamming, bootleg records and the Topsy hit
17.q: No, a student brought that same record by and showed it to me, but I didn't know anything about it. Last one I saw was up there on MGM. This is new. Now of course the only thing that they eliminated on this one, it wasn't a Cozy Conception of Carmen, it's just Cozy Cole.

146.t: Never receiving royalties for One O'Clock Jump
146.s: Smith says he made up One O'Clock Jump with Basie at the Reno Club and never got royalties or even a credit.
146.q: Well, trust the man. You see, I made the number up... It was in the Reno Club with Basie...

146.t: Basie's royalties and Eddie Durham's payout
146.s: Basie gets royalties every year while Eddie Durham told Smith he got a one-time payment.
146.q: Last time, Eddie Durham told me that he went down there and the record company gave him... Of course, it's so old, and he got $16,000/$68,000(?). Walked out. That's why I'm going back to New York.

146.t: Atlantic session in 1959 and the Floyd Dixon album in 1960
146.s: Atlantic was the only session Smith was paid for; a 1960 Fort Worth album with Floyd Dixon went unpaid, and they discuss his band including drummer Robert Cobbs.
146.ch: Technique, jam sessions, audiences and records
146.q: I didn't get nothin'. Not a dime. Didn't get a thing. The only one I got paid for recording was the Atlantic Recording Company.

146.t: Fraudulent record companies and lost 1949 records
146.s: Smith says most small record men were frauds who vanished, and he found his own records on jukeboxes; he cut a 1949 session with Cooper and never was paid.
146.ch: Technique, jam sessions, audiences and records
146.q: No, no. All them went under the headin' of some of them big recording companies around the country. And see, some of them was frauds. The big majority of them was frauds. The band was (?)moving on(?) recording, and they listened to them, and the union got behind them and said, "Now, if you don't…

69.t: Perdido's success and late payments from Tempo
69.s: Tizol says Perdido and Caravan were his best tunes and he was shortchanged on royalties; he and Rose complain that Tempo, run by Duke's sister, pays late.
69.ch: Caravan, Perdido and the first tunes
69.q: have no business getting nothing, but later on in the years, he gave me a percentage on Caravan, which has been the two best things for me -- that was Caravan and Perdifo. And that old sonofabitch, that sister of Duke Ellington, you know -- she was the one who messed me up.

69.t: How he got a royalty share in Caravan
69.s: Irving Mills gave him a percentage on Caravan in return for his other tunes, with two cheques a year; his name was always going to be on it.
69.ch: Caravan, Perdido and the first tunes
69.q: Oh, I don't know; I forgot now what it was. But I know he wanted a contract to all my tunes, to get them over to Mills and this and the other, so he said, 'Well, if you leave all those tunes in here, I will give you a percentage now on Caravan.' So they gave me a percentage -- I forgot the…

69.t: Pérez Prado's Patricia and the unsuit
69.s: He says Pérez Prado took the first part of Perdido for his hit Patricia; Tempo wanted him to sue but he let it go because Prado had copied others.
69.ch: Caravan, Perdido and the first tunes
69.q: No. They asked me why I don't sue him, but he had been stealing numbers from everybody, so then he was allowed later on, to sue me, so I said, oh, well,

69.t: Unreleased tunes and publishers Robbins, Leeds and Mills
69.s: He gave tunes to Robbins and Leeds and five to Mills and heard nothing; Willard offers Mills's address.
69.q: No, I don't remember myself. Oh, I did so many things like a fool, and I gave it to so many publishers; I gave it to Robbins Rollins, I gave it to Leefs, and I never hear about it -- like I told you before, these five tunes, which I would like to one of these days, if you tell me how to get to…

385.t: Sonet royalties on Tiny's Exercise and the 1977 date
385.s: He complains that Sonet paid him a thousand dollars for a 1977 session and never any royalties, and wants it printed.
385.ch: Chords, recordings and his own groups
385.q: ... It went over pretty good. But like, boy, the royalties that are being taken from the black man is pitiful... The people just take. They don't even have the courtesy -- Sonet does have the courtesy to send you a thing that's always wrong,

385.t: How Hawkins and Parker took over his dates
385.s: He suggested Hawkins and Parker and then found their names as leaders; he had to fight for the leader's fee.
385.q: Q You made a nice record with J.C. Higginbotham-- do you remember much about that at all? Yeah well see, I procured... I got them a lot of musicians that were idle and could use a gig. Like Coleman Hawkins wasn't doin' nothin'. And I suggested him, I said "I think I could get Coleman Hawkins"…

385.t: Aftermath: Parker given the next date, reissues under the star's name
385.s: Lubinsky said they had a million dollars in hand, then gave Parker the next date without Grimes, and later reissues put Parker, and Hawkins, first.
385.q: The funny part after we made this record date and I convinced Lubinsky to hire it, he came to me later and said, 'Did you know we had a million dollars in our hands and didn't know what to do with it.' I said 'You had the million. I didn't have the million, I knew what to do with it, cause I kept…

385.t: Pay for the Parker date and royalties
385.s: The date paid union scale, forty-four dollars for sidemen and eighty-eight for the leader, with small royalties still coming from Arista.
385.q: ... Union scale... $44 for sidemen, $88 for the leader... I have recievd a few royalties through Arista label, they bought the company... As far back as that was I still get a few schecks, ha ha...

168.t: Secretly recorded by Rosenkrantz and never paid royalties
168.s: The audience cheered, then Rosenkrantz revealed he had taped them; the Commodore release was a big seller but they got no royalties.
168.ch: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
168.q: And that went over -- we finished out, finally finished the number, and the audience stood up and gave us such a round of applause, you know. It was so wonderful. Then, of course, we did another number which was called "I've Got Rhythm," and that was it. That lasted for at least -- it could have…

168.t: Recording business, royalties, and Flat Foot Floogie
168.s: Stewart says recordings were not much of a rip-off in his time and that royalties on Flat Foot Floogie were his best; Crouch sees it anticipating Louis Jordan.
168.q: Well, I don't think it could be compared to nowadays, you know, the rip-off department and what have you. They weren't too bad, what I mean, I might say. I was well paid for my recording, my -- even with my groups and what have you.

168.t: Tunes from a studio session credited to someone else; ASCAP
168.s: Claire Stewart explains that about ten tunes he improvised in the studio were credited to another name, and they told ASCAP the royalties belong to Slam.
168.q: Well, he -- I would say there are probably ten songs that he came up with in the studio that he named and are -- on the record, are given credit as Ogner Bozer (PHONETIC). Now, ASCAP has received a letter that they want to claim the royalties on it.

168.t: Bootleg recordings at European concerts and the Black and Blue label
168.s: Stewart complains about audience members taping performances in Europe and says his problems are with Black and Blue.
168.q: Yes, that is quite a problem. I remember on two or three occasions when I appeared in France and different parts of Europe, even in Germany, Denmark, Switzerland, where when we were appearing and performing, we'd run across situations where we were being recorded by someone in the audience. Somehow…

238.t: Always owing the record company and signing without advice
238.s: She says artists never get out of debt to record companies and she, like others, signed without managers or lawyers.
238.q: always owe the record company. You owe them all the time. You never get out of debt with the record company. Well, this was a bad scene to start with, because years ago, you know -- see today, when they get an artist today, or get kids recording today, well, they put out an awful lot of cash money,…

238.t: Her first Capitol contract: flat fee and promised royalty
238.s: Her first Capitol contract was non-royalty, a flat fee per record with a promised royalty if it hit, before Carlos Gastel became her manager.
238.q: Well, frankly, some of the things, yes, I did. However, my very first contract with Capitol, for instance, was a non-royalty contract. However, this was a temporary contract. This was --

238.t: Feeling taken advantage of; publishing and ASCAP
238.s: She feels Capitol took her creative material under a poor contract; she still owns part of the Hurry On Down copyright and praises ASCAP.
238.q: Yeah, all of those things are recorded. They wanted to record it, see, they wanted to record the music. But as I say, the point is it was unfair in a way for me to have-- for them to have gotten this material from me and then put me under a lousy contract or something, you see. I feel like this is…

238.t: Hurry On Down as a flat-fee hit
238.s: Hurry On Down was recorded for a flat fee with a promised better contract, which manager Carlos Gastel later arranged.
238.ch: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
238.q: Well, I don't recall getting -- I don't recall at that time getting it, but when I got a manager -- I did not have a manager at that time -- Carlos Gastel, when he came on the scene he changed all of that. He changed the contract and changed, you know, saw to it that I did get it.

1046.t: Dave Bartholomew's trust and who gets producer credit
1046.s: Quezergue discusses working for Dave, who gave him tasks but stayed in the studio; he complains that money-men get producer credit over the person doing the work.
1046.q: I don't really worry about it. No. Oh, that, I don't know. He gave it to me, yeah. I would say in a sense, yes. In a sense that, you know, here, I want you to do this, I want you to do this and do that. And I said, get together with, say, get together with Earl, or get together with Bernie Dean,…

1046.t: How NOLA and Malaco sessions were financed; Barefootin' origins
1046.s: Partners paid for sessions, musicians were paid more after hits; Robert Parker brought the song Barefootin', which sat on the shelf and was released on Eugene Welly's label.
1046.q: Well, we all, we all, we all, we all put up the money. Uh, you know, sometimes some of the musicians, uh, did it for, uh, some of the musicians did it for, uh, for not for the right, uh, right amount of money. Uh, for instance, like, it must have been, uh, it must have been, uh, a barefootin'. Like…

1046.s: Atlantic thought Barefootin' was theirs under a deal; threats of a lawsuit came to nothing, and NOLA distributed it itself.
1046.q: Yeah, but that wasn't the one that we had to deal with. This came back, we were late in the game, that with this Walker fellow, we had a record of something called, uh, uh, Pelican, or was it Pelican? We had a group, some of the same people called Pelican, and he had his own label, the Walker…

780.t: Royalties from Chess and signing a contract while underage
780.s: The second record made money; he bought suits and went to New York, and he should not have signed a contract at his age.
780.ch: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
780.q: Ico, no I don't think so. I was pretty young when I was doing those records. Yeah. So I wasn't really responsible. In fact, I shouldn't have signed a contract. Yeah.

780.s: He got nothing from the Dixie Cups' version because he was not credited as writer and it was never copyrighted.
780.ch: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
780.q: No, the copyright never expired. It was never copyrighted. It was never copyrighted.

780.t: Being recorded unknowingly at WMRY for five dollars
780.s: His first record was cut at the radio station without his knowing it was a recording, paid five dollars and released without a contract.
780.ch: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
780.q: We went around a couple of blocks away. Bought us some red beans and rice and got us some wine. That was it. In fact, I didn't know the record was going to be released. Nobody did, really.

760.t: The Jones-Collins Astoria Hot Eight recordings at Italian Hall
760.s: He describes the Astoria band, its personnel, and giving each leader one of his tunes for the records.
760.q: I played with the band regularly. I played at the, the band used to play at this club right here where the post office is on Bienville. It was named the, I call it the club not so long ago we used to talk. Well anyway we were.

760.t: Lost record contracts and unpaid royalties
760.s: No one can produce the contracts, so the band could not collect thousands of dollars in royalties.
760.q: Yeah, well that was, that was my tune, Tip Easy blues. That's the one I've taken and I give damp weather blues to Poirnell I think it was, either Sydney. I know I gave them two, two numbers and.

760.t: Origin of the tune You Don't Love Me and the True lawsuit
760.s: He traces the tune from Celestin's and Ridgley's bands to Don Albert and Paul Gayten and the royalties dispute.
760.q: I made Duke Ellington's Ringin' Bells. Oh yeah, I remember that. And I put that on. And I'll tell you about those recordings. Then I was the first one made this number, You Don't Love Me. You see the right name wasn't You Don't Love Me. That's the name of Paul Gaithin made it and called it True.

1011.s: Conniff received 'Begin the Beguine' as a single and signed a stock Columbia contract at three percent of the record price, netting about eighteen cents an album.
1011.q: anyway, so we did the Rosie sessions, and you asked — I still didn’t answer the question about the deal. So anyway when we got back — oh Mitch says I’m going to make it up to you when we get back, when we get back to New York. So that’s what he did. He gave me that single that I told you about,…

1011.t: Flat artist deal, recording costs and top royalty
1011.s: Mitch Miller raised him to the five percent top royalty; Conniff explains recording budgets then and now and that selling product gets a good deal.
1011.q: would come out. I never worried about what was in the contract. So it finally got up where I got — I was what they called in those days a flat artist. In other words, I used to go in, they’d pay the cost of my musicians and singers, which was a big item you know — well in those days it wasn’t that…

1011.s: Conniff wasted two years with attorneys trying to stop imitators before moving on; only James Last survived by developing his own style.
1011.q: Oh yeah, there were a lot of them. As a matter of fact I wasted about two years of my life trying to find a way to stop them from doing it. And I had attorneys and copyright attorneys and regular attorneys, and we did a lot of research. We found out, they found out that I couldn’t — it’s different…

1012.s: Whether the estate earns from samples of Skull Sessions, depends on who owns the music, and a pianist's album of his father's tunes without clearance.
1012.q: They do if we own it. That’s the issue. To make sure that we own what they’re sampling see. Because if they sample with Universal stuff then we’ll get some but we’ll get half of

1012.t: Resolving the Bela Fleck Hoedown copyright issue
1012.s: Fleck's recording used his father's Hoedown; Nelson Jr. settled by having Fleck pay his attorney and record father's tunes in Indianapolis.
1012.q: Oh yeah. And actually I did have one I have to share with you. Bela Fleck, the great banjo player, he did an album called “Out Bound” this was several years ago. So my attorney now went to hear Bela play and they did “Hoedown.” So Aaron Copland’s “Hoedown” is owned by somebody else. So they did…

1012.t: Taking over the estate, the LLC and Stolen Moments rights
1012.s: After the stepmother's death he and his brother formed an LLC, he sued a publisher, and he explains how his father sold the rights to Stolen Moments for 700 dollars.
1012.q: Well you’re fighting, what good is it going to do? You know what I mean? It just doesn’t make any sense at all. And then I’ve had a couple of — I had to learn the business of music on the fly because my stepmother basically controlled everything until she died. So

61.t: Conkling cuts the 12-inch LP price; publishers balk
61.s: Columbia priced 12-inch LPs at $3.98 by persuading publishers to lower royalties; only Herman Starr refused.
61.ch: Erroll Garner and the long-playing revolution
61.q: felt that even $4.98 is too much, because we were ready to cut, and I believe we did cut, about that time, the Masterworks price down to $4.95. Not $4.98. I don’t know why, but the tax worked out that way at that time. We wanted to have a $3.95 LP. We did it with the copyright problem being solved…

61.t: Structuring the Rollins advance: royalty rates and tax years
61.s: The statutory 2-cent license on long pieces and splitting the payment across tax years made the big advance work.
61.ch: RCA years: Rollins, Nero and singers
61.q: Yeah, unheard of. But we were talking a three-year contract, and I had a kind of – two aces in the hole, which people didn’t think about, especially people not in the music business. One was that clause in the statutory rate at the time, for publishers to license copyrights at 2 cents regardless of…

61.t: Herman Starr's printout and long jazz performances
61.s: Starr proved he earned more royalties anyway; longer LP tracks saved royalties and opened a door for jazz; RCA's 45 story.
61.ch: Erroll Garner and the long-playing revolution
61.q: This was before computers, but these machines still ground out these accordion-pleated papers. He said, “I just want to show you the royalties that I got from you this year compared to last year.” He said, “I got more money this year when you said that you weren’t going to record my music than you…

133.t: Love of standards; Horace Silver pieces and royalty checks
133.s: Asked about his standards repertoire, Walton cites Nat King Cole and Ellington, then talks about the royalty income that still trickles in, including a 28 cent check.
133.ch: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
133.q: Uh, indirectly and partially, yeah. But I was drawn to 'em anyway, you know, because uh, Nat King Cole, Sweet Lorraine, those pieces were indelibly in my memory too. The standard I just couldn't live without, I couldn't go … Well, let's see, Ellington's pieces were standards, but uh … uh or…

133.t: Publishing: Harry Fox, BMI, his own company and business advice
133.s: He explains Harry Fox, BMI and his own publishing company that gives an annual guarantee, and says Benny Golson and Gigi Gryce advised him that in jazz publishing just means ownership.
133.q: Oh man, let me see. Quite a few years. And uh, one advantage of that is that every October, which happens to be now [chuckles], they give you a … if they can see uh to their uh whatever monitoring system they have that you, uh, uh, uh, your recording, your compositions, uh, are being recorded,…

133.t: The money: $7,500 flat plus $1,500 per arrangement
133.s: At Brower's prompting Walton reveals Columbia paid $7,500 flat plus $1,500 per arrangement, about nineteen thousand for one project, with continuing publishing royalties.
133.ch: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
133.q: Okay. Uh, for that period in, in, in, uh my life, uh, which was in the '70s – '70s slash '80s. Yeah, uh … So you got, it encompasses the '70s and the '80s, uh …. Well, let's see here; it might say so on here. But these amounts that I'm about to reveal [laughs] were uh, flat pay was $7,500 just,…

137.t: ASCAP royalties and checking record company books
137.s: Royalties from Basie material and air shots were once as high as $1,700 a check, then fell as ASCAP paid new rock and roll writers; auditing record company books is hopeless.
137.ch: Long Island years and Battle's estate
137.q: I wasn't doing any writing then but was heavy. the was heavy (unintelligible). My checks sometime would be as high as $1700.

137.t: No money from the million-selling Part Two Topsy
137.s: Durham says he never got paid on the Topsy hit because of a publisher mix-up with Love Records and Cliff Records.
137.ch: Long Island years and Battle's estate
137.q: Well, publisher. Battles with the publisher. He told me that Love Records had that and they went bankrupt. I just found out two years ago that that was all Cliff Records, because Phil ________ told me. He say,

137.t: Sharing composer credit to get songs recorded
137.s: Durham argues that giving half a song to a big name was worth it, discussing Fats Waller, Hodges and Ellington and the obstacles for black writers.
137.q: You know why? Because they don't go back and write another one. As soon as you do that, then you go back and you write something else. If you can write another one, you don't worry too much. But the guy that can't write -- that'll never get nothing else, he's the one that's crazy.

566.t: 'Ebobaleeba' and 'Million Dollar Secret': hits and credit disputes
566.s: Humes and Dance sort out the late-1940s hits. 'Ebobaleeba' was her only royalty; 'Million Dollar Secret' for Modern was recorded at the Shrine, and the recording man put his name on it until Mr. Koenig got it removed.
566.q: I don't remember that. But I know I made it, and the man who recorded it, he put his name on it. It was supposed to be his number. And then Mr. Koenig had a terrible time getting his name off of it.

566.t: Black and Blue's objection to her Montreux festival appearance
566.s: At Montreux in 1974 the Black and Blue people objected and brought an attorney, though Humes said she had no contract and would not sing her Black and Blue songs.
566.q: And he came and he didn't want me to do any of the songs that I had done for Black and Blue. I said, 'well I won't do that.' And so one of the first people I saw when I got to the festival was Nan and he had his attorney with him. He said, 'I brought my attorney'. I said, 'well you didn't need no…

566.t: Peggy Lee and how much of her came from Billie
566.s: Humes met Peggy Lee in California, who sang her baby to sleep with 'Ebobaleeba'. Dance says Peggy took much from Billie Holiday and made millions while Billie struggled; Humes shrugs that is the business.
566.q: Yeah, she is. And I remember the first time I came out to California, I went to a recording session of her's. And she said, 'Oh Helen, I'm just so glad to see you'. She had just had a little baby, you know.

386.t: Re-recording the same songs, and a pension idea for musicians
386.s: Because royalties never arrive he records many versions of the same tunes, and proposes that long-time musicians get an annuity.
386.ch: Decca, Cow Cow Blues and royalties
386.q: to him that he do to me. I play the same song that I made on another record so he ain't got a damn thing. Just got another version of a song I made. I got five versions of "Honeysuckle Rose," you know that? I got "Willow Weep For Me" three or four times on records. These are things that I've…

386.t: Royalty quarrels with Sidney Bechet and Jimmy Rushing
386.s: He describes how he and Jimmy Rushing fell out over money from 'Leave Me' and 'How You Want Your Lovin' Done'.
386.ch: Decca, Cow Cow Blues and royalties
386.q: And so does BMI. And so does the union, but they, they, you know,...but I made a lot of records and got nothing. Absolutely nothing. Well I did a thing with Sidney Bechet. I wrote the tune; I said, "Sidney, man, you got half of it.." you know, I'm not liberal. I wrote Same with Jimmy Rushing.…

386.t: Copyright, royalties and unpaid London records
386.s: He argues that musicians deserve royalties and describes unpaid songs on his London record.
386.q: And when a guy go out and give an assignment to go write...to write and assignment, they more than likely, if he has any brains, will give him some money to get picture rights, or to get the right to use the name, something...and I just don't think that people should use your material like that in…

454.t: Royalties: Carla Bley, Brubeck and Paul Desmond
454.s: Argument about whether white jazz musicians do better; Johnson says the record business steals from everyone.
454.ch: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
454.q: He said that when he oversaw the latest (Inaudible) contract with Paul Desmond, Paul did start getting artist royalties and very quickly.

454.t: Debut Records and keeping control of his publishing
454.s: Mingus ran his own label and publishing because he saw what happened to others.
454.ch: Pedal points, Hampton, Norvo and Debut
454.q: Yeah, because I could see what they were doing to other people.

454.t: The unpublished portion of Beneath the Underdog
454.s: Mingus wants Sue to edit the cut material about record-company theft and Debut sales.
454.ch: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
454.q: theft, about the record companies and all that. How I sold records for Debut Records, and they never sold as many as I did myself. Some of the things we're talking about now with Sy. That's why that book will be interesting.

31.t: Louis Prima and Keely Smith copying 'White Cliffs of Dover'
31.s: Whaley says Louis Prima had his Apollo staging of 'White Cliffs of Dover' copied and published it as his own.
31.ch: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
31.q: So we had -- Costin, she was a ingenue and we had White Cliffs of Dover and we had the girls singing against it, you know, like a kind of melody, they'd sing the kind of melody and she'd sing the melody and they would fill in with words, so Louis Prima got somebody to sit in the audience to copy…

31.t: Claude Hopkins publishes Whaley's 'I'd Do Almost Anything for You'
31.s: Whaley says he wrote the number at the Lafayette, handed the score to Claude Hopkins, and it was published by Hopkins, Williams and Joe Davis.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: Claude came by -- I had wrote a number, I'd Do Almost Anything for You -- and it became a big hit, Bill Robinson, Jive Smith, Charlie Parker, they all sang it, and the people would start coming up to it and they'd stop.

31.t: The 'White Cliffs of Dover' copying story again
31.s: He retells how a white trumpet-player bandleader copied the Apollo show's 'White Cliffs of Dover' and recorded it.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: No. He was a trumpet player and a singer -- oh, what's his name. He died a few months ago, he was in the hospital a long while, and he had that girl who used to sing with him. Anyway, 'White Cliffs of Dover' was a big number and his band was playing it, and he told all of his band men to copy their…

7.t: Ending the studio; publishing; BMI deal; losing his Joe Davis rights
7.s: The studio lasts two years, a publishing firm folds, and Thomas explains how he lost royalties on his Joe Davis records.
7.ch: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
7.q: We had it about two years. But Cozy kept going in and out of town. And we had a publishing company, but Cozy never did...he never did contribute to the publishing company, so it just went kerplunk. I had a good deal, too. And I wrote his book, but I didn't give him a chance to write my books. I had…

7.t: How reissues of his records cost him royalties
7.s: He recounts handing over scores, a lost letter promising royalties from Prestige, a collector's cleaned-up tape, and being swindled, like Jelly.
7.ch: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
7.q: Yes. I guess I picked it up from Jelly Roll. I was just so happy to be recording... And then another guy that was... How can I put it? He was a fan of mine. He collected the records, and he's the one that got the idea of putting it on an album. He took it and got as much of the surface noise...…

7.t: Moe Gale's 'holding company' and late recording payments
7.s: The band was paid a year after recording, with Gale keeping the interest.
7.ch: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
7.q: I remember that time we made...we recorded with Cab, and they paid us a year later, on Christmas, like it was a big deal. You know, originally we called Gale a holding company. That was the name of the company, 'holding company' -- and boy, they could hold money. And we got so mad that year... We…

78.t: Dealing with music publishers: selling outright and exclusive contracts
78.s: Horace sold some originals outright, signed an exclusive contract that let tunes gather dust, and learned to demand cancellation clauses; Fletcher was too trusting.
78.ch: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
78.q: Well, there were a few companies that I dealt with that I sold the originals outright, unfortunately, before I got hip, you know, to what I should have done. There were others that we had a deal where there it was a commission thing going on, you know. And then -- let's see -- there was a company…

78.t: How Chu Berry got the credit and Joe Davis made a fortune
78.s: Sixty bands recorded it before Fletcher. Horace had not copyrighted it, publisher Joe Davis bought it outright from Chu Berry and earned over $100,000, and Horace later wrote 'Chris and His Gang'.
78.ch: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
78.q: Yeah, it wasn't like the millions they're talking about now. But I tell you, I remember an incident about this particular tune. I didn't have it copyrighted or anything. I just went on and did the arrangement, I was tickled to death with it. know. And, of course, Tom, I was yelling about these…

78.t: Other near-miss hits: 'Hot and Anxious' and the riff that became 'Castle Rock'
78.s: At Chicago's Circle Inn, Al Sears' men paid $5 requests for Horace's riff while writing it down, and it appeared on record as 'Castle Rock'.
78.ch: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
78.q: I wrote another tune called 'Hot and Anxious,' and this was taken away with some more riffs. I wrote another thing with a guy listening at me play it in Chicago at a club called the Circle Inn. 451.q: Yeah. I can’t remember that specifically, but, but it has come in handy and every once in a while I’ll get, as you know, get a nice royalty check so that’s worked out great. Thank you for that.

165.s: Royalties were withheld by publishers; he recalls Churchill Coleman and says he is still chasing money.
165.q: I’m still chasing those people. I’m still chasing them. I saw Churchill Coleman, who wrote Cry, in front of the Brill Building asking for $2 to get back home to Philadelphia. He’d just had the big hit by Johnny Rae. He’d gone to the publisher. The publisher had told him that there were no…

704.t: Owning your publishing: Billy Taylor, returning Horace Silver's tunes, Milken
704.s: Jones says Billy Taylor taught him about ownership, he gave back Horace Silver's and Marvin Hamlisch's songs, mentions gurus Irving Green, Steve Ross and Mike Milken, and shows Milken's multiplication trick.
704.q: Oh yeah. Singularly Billy Taylor. There’s nobody else to talk about. Gigi was aware of it too, but it was Billy Taylor that really laid it on me, I think in 1954. Early. That’s why I had Horace’s – I had five of Horace’s tunes. I had Benny Golson. I did Whisper Not, Along Came Betty, all that…

226.t: Learning the publishing business and explaining it to artists
226.s: He explains that artists signed away publishing at record sessions, and how Cannonball and associates helped bring writers to Gopam.
226.ch: Cannonball Adderley and John Levy Enterprises
226.q: My first experience as far as the publishing business was with George Shearing. From the very beginning, he was the first person that I could establish a relationship with in terms of – thinking in terms of the publishing business. He wasn’t aware of what was going on, and none of the other people…

589.t: Relationship with Phil and Leonard Chess; Daddy-O's business advice
589.s: Lewis has no horror story about Chess; Daddy-O Daylie advised him to want royalty statements and advances rather than cars or watches.
589.q: I think that Daddy-O Daylie – Holmes Daylie was his name. His personality, his radio name, was Daddy-O. He was an advantage to us in many ways. Our business with the Chess people, fortunately Daddy-O, not that he was our business representative, but he would always say, “Make sure you” and then…

492.t: Atlantic royalties and Forest Flower: just businessmen
492.s: Asked by Indian fans about Forest Flower, Lloyd says he got ten cents a dance, no real royalties, and left because he did not believe in the plantation system.
492.ch: The Village, Big Sur and leaving the business
492.q: Amazing. I mean she spent eight years on that, plus the fact that she’s thirty or forty getting ready for that. Anyway, so these people wanted to know about, and they said, “What was it like?” I said, “Well, you know, I was recording for Atlantic and they...” They were talking about the Forest…

228.t: Blue Note reissues and who owns his music
228.s: Blue Note issues unreleased sessions without asking him, and catalogs get sold on to firms like Coca Cola.
228.ch: Later Blue Note years and ending the habit
228.q: No, man, they don’t ask you nothing. They don’t even send you a record. They don’t even send you a CD in the mail and say, “Thanks a lot. We’re letting this out.” You just hear somebody say, “Hey, man, I just picked up a new CD by you called” whatever.

408.t: Not selling out, and not asking for a point
408.s: Why he never advertised the Billy Joel solo and missed royalty points.
408.ch: Pop sessions and the hit-record question
408.q: Never count your royalties until the chickens come home, baby. So I, you know, easy bread. But yeah, I mean I mean the Billy Joel thing I got more attention, you know, but I never, I never felt like using it in my publicity because I mean the people that had been following my career, and I go way…

374.t: Worries about repeating stories, and the book's first publication in 1953
374.s: Russell asks whether his stories could bother relatives; Daughtry recaps the check and the 1953 publication.
374.ch: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
374.q: Yeah. Eventually Buckwheat recovered. He was extremely embarrassed by it. I think – well, he certainly learned a lesson. But he also passed away young. So all those people, somehow they died young.

63.t: Recording pay: advances, scale and royalties; Beguine as albatross
63.s: RCA paid $1,000 per selection, musicians got scale, royalties came only after recoupment; Beguine paid for houses and divorces.
63.ch: Own bands: swing concert, Brunswick, RCA
63.q: No, it was my band. The record company gave me in those days a $1,000 advance per selection. If we’d go into a record session, three-hour session, union scale, the band got 25 bucks and we recorded four tunes. I got 4,000 bucks and the band got 17 times 25 or 18 times 25, whatever it was. That was…

509.t: The Mercury contract, artistic control and royalties
509.s: At Mercury under Quincy she had artistic control and royalties; she declines to discuss Verve Polygram.
509.q: With Mercury, yes. I was very happy with them. There was no problems. I had complete artistic control, and there was Quincy there, who saw about me, you know, so there were no problems.

375.t: Ben Tucker, 'I'm Comin' Home, Baby' and Herbie Mann's Notice of Use case
375.s: Talk of who wrote the song, the Notice of Use court case over the first recording, and Bobby Hebb's lack of business savvy.
375.q: ...recorded it, and he was in court. There was a court thing, and it was hinging on the first recording, whoever recorded it at first, and the Notice of Use... They straightened all that stuff out since then. Even if you had a copyright, the Notice of Use thing could be a roadblock. So he had to…

376.t: Doing his own management and Bluesette royalties
376.s: He managed himself; Jimmy Smith's Bluesette album sold 100,000 copies.
376.q: Yes. I did [inaudible] there. But I had one lucky break. I was composing, you know, of course, and I had written Bluesette, which was never a major hit. But a hit goes like that, and Bluesette is the kind of song as… [inaudible] and Jimmy Smith had recorded Bluesette. And once 100,000 copies,…

136.t: The album title and the 'Toshiko's Blues' credit
136.s: Brown reads the discography; she says the blues was really Bud Powell's tune and Granz's credit caused her trouble.
136.ch: The Ginza live house and the Granz recording
136.q: Is it? No, Amazing, I don‟t think that was the one, though. I think the first one was a 10-inch [LP], the pink … the cover, [there was] a flower coming out of the piano.

109.t: Jim Chapin's book on his style
109.s: Jim Chapin wrote a book on Clarke's left-hand and foot work that sold worldwide, with no royalties for Clarke, though drummers needed to see it to believe it.
109.ch: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
109.q: One drummer who liked it, Jim Chapin, who liked it so much he wrote a book, and that opened the whole thing up to everybody.

614.t: Columbia's free hand and the Sinatra-level publicity deal
614.s: Columbia, under Manny Sachs, gave him freedom; he asked for the same publicity as Sinatra and Dinah Shore rather than money.
614.ch: Decca years and the First Herd
614.q: Very. And, of course, I was there during a period which was not a long one, where a guy -- Manny Sachs, who was Sinatra's man, and he liked music and he had a flare for putting good things together. And very few suggestions, other than, 'Can I do something for you?'

677.t: Pay only for days worked and shelved records
677.s: He learned he was paid only for days worked with expenses on him, did not reach $100 until 1938-39, and unreleased records went unpaid.
677.q: Oh, they were -- most of them, see, with our tips, with our movies, with our records, by that time I'd made a couple records, with the Quality Serenaders, and $70.00 a week, that was nothing. Of course, that was the beginning of many, many, many surprises. The first one was I didn't know -- I…

88.t: Lee plans to publish Lester's songs to get royalties to his family
88.s: Lee says companies exploit deceased musicians without accounting to the estate, and says he will copyright Lester's songs in his Flipside publishing company for Lester Jr.
88.q: I'll tell you something on this tape -- and then I'm gonna close out with this. But let me tell you something. I'm in the recording business, right? I think and I see where musicians that are deceased, I think it's just criminal what the record companies do and the people that have the masters,…

4.t: BMI and the planned publishing company with Jelly Roll
4.s: In the late 1930s BMI courted the Spikes catalog but they stayed with ASCAP; Spikes and Jelly Roll planned a new publishing firm until Jelly Roll died.
4.q: in about '38 or in '39, I think it was, the BMI Music Association was opening up to try to be like ASCAP, and they sent for us, and we went out there and they wanted us to come in with them 'cause we had a catalog, you know. They didn't have nobody with any catalog of music so we told them no, we…

9.t: Recording pay and who handled the business
9.s: Record pay came months later via the leader with no bonus; Russell handled the business and musicians simply received what they were promised.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: : It would be from three to six months gettin' paid. Three to six months later. No, you didn't get it then and there. But I think we did get paid for "Can't Give You Anything But Love." We got paid right away for that. I think so, yeah. But the rest of the numbers, we had to wait until they did the…

89.t: Record pay, Perry Bradford's royalties and record prices
89.s: Musicians got a flat thirty dollars per record while the writer of Crazy Blues reportedly made ninety thousand dollars in royalties; records sold for seventy-five cents.
89.q: Well, they just fixed -- $30.00 a record. And you played two sides. You got $30.00 for it. If it took you six hours it was $30.00. If it took you two hours it was $30.00. That was the price.

167.t: Royalties, selling tunes outright and not worrying about the business
167.s: He got small royalties from "I've Come a Long Ways, Baby", sold tunes to publishers for a flat fee, and just wanted his check.
167.q: And then I'd have a lot of record dates. By somebody else. They'd take me on the date and I'd wait for my check to come in when it was due, you know.

90.t: Murray Rappaport's label and the lawsuit
90.s: His first recordings on Murray Rappaport's label, a shady dealing and a lost court case; Rappaport later jailed.
90.q: it was just about 1947 when I made my first recordings on my own. At the time he called the label MGM, and so MGM made him give up that title, and so then he named it Rem, and he changed it from Rem to Rex... But anyway, the things that I did...

381.t: Clyde Otis, the rhythm section and passing up contractor money
381.s: Clyde Otis let him set rhythms but was annoyed he gave the contracting to Frank Carroll and earned scale.
381.q: Well, as a contractor. I gave the contracting to somebody else; he wanted me to be the contractor, and I said, I don't want it, and at the time, I gave it to Frank Carroll because I was doing all of Frank Carroll's work. So instead of me making the money, Frank Carroll was making the money and I…

382.t: Not getting copies of her records or being paid
382.s: She had to buy her own copy, sent copies home to Pittsburgh, never knew a side was released, and doubts she was paid.
382.ch: Early recordings and arrival in New York
382.q: Yes. It came up because I -- as I said before -- I had just come to New York. I don't think I'd been in New York two months when that was made. And I came to New York from Pittsburgh. So the club that I was working in, I sent about ten copies back to Pittsburgh. And I got a note that it was number…

453.t: Recording fees and the manager Johnny Collins
453.s: Randolph thinks the band was shortchanged on the cartoon, short and records by Collins, whom he and DeMichael suspect was a crook; Glaser later paid off Collins.
453.q: Well, I -- to really tell you the truth, the recording fee -- I don't think we really got due justice on it, because Mike -- as I told you, I had charge of the arranging part of it, and directing the music -- I mean, the music director, and Mike had done most of the managing, like getting the…

93.t: Teddy Hale's bolero tap to Begin the Beguine
93.s: Green recalls Hale wanting to tap the Begin the Beguine bolero, popularised by Eddie Heywood's recording; the talk drifts into royalties and unions.
93.q: Well that's what he was into, it was a reintroduced. See? He's going to do something else now, he's he probably was trying to surprise me, you know, which he did. You see? It's co -- like a corporation getting subpoenaed, you know. And they want to know why we're being subpoenaed, you know, and…

94.t: The Pumpkin label bootleg of Bechet in Boston
94.s: He learns of a bootleg LP from 1951 and talks about bootlegs and unpaid musicians.
94.ch: Sidney Bechet and the Paris festival
94.q: And I intend to tape this and some day maybe I will -- since everybody else is taping to make albums, I think I'll tape some of this and make my own album. What can they do to me? What can they do to those guys? I couldn't do anything with these guys for the Pocket labels, you know.

384.t: Irving Mills, publishing and the Master Records sides
384.s: Mills printed everything Morehouse wrote and issued his Master sides; Morehouse says tunes like Plastered in Paris and Blues in B Flat were his, while Mills put his own name on everything.
384.ch: Hutto 1978-79: NBC, radio and the N'goma drums
384.q: That's right. And he was in the Roseland building upon on Broadway. So everything that I'd write, I'd take right down to Irving Mills.

387.t: RCA, tour financing and original material
387.q: I know that they do it, but they only do it under duress. They never really want to, they're forced to do it, and obviously they weren't in those days.

19.t: Sir Charles Thompson and the dispute over Robbins' Nest
19.s: Thompson left after getting no credit or royalties on the hit tune, which opened the job for Malachi.
19.ch: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
19.q: I got there and I found out Sir Charles had quit because of a misunderstanding that he had with Illinois over a tune that he had written called "Robbins Nest." It seems as if Illinois had recorded the tune, and I don't know who named it after Fred Robbins, the disk jockey there... So they called it…

74.t: McGuinney's in Sheepshead Bay and not getting Amen royalties
74.s: Amen is famous by summer 1942, but Mayo Williams's threats keep Mosley from claiming and he gets no royalties.
74.ch: Queens Terrace, Decca records and Amen
74.q: We went in there and by that time "Amen" had gotten famous, it was very famous then, and also Woody Herman had put it in a picture called "What's Cooking".

6.t: His first record with J. C. Johnson
6.s: He again names J. C. Johnson as his first recording and they chat about composers being ripped off by publishers.
6.ch: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
6.q: Oh, my first record was back, way back. I remember this record I made with J. C., that's it, J. C. Johnson. That's what they called him, J. C. J. C. Johnson. Yes, he's a -- I understand he's living upstate someplace right now.

389.t: Venuti, Sudhalter and the Williams College Whiteman library
389.s: Others copied his Whiteman arrangements from Williams College and performed them in England without paying him.
389.q: Venuti. He had traveled all over Europe and he told me that he could get anything he wanted over there in the way of musicians and Sudhalter even wanted me to go to England and do it. 'You could get good musicians over there' and he did some concerts over there and called me up from England and…

125.t: Royalties, Robin's Nest credit and bad contracts
125.s: Thompson got paid only for the dates, shared Robin's Nest credit with Jacquet, and says artists signed contracts leaving songs out of their hands, like Fats Waller.
125.q: Definitely not. In fact I didn't get any money at all. I got paid for the date and I didn't get any money for -- which is a sad part of my life. But unfortunately I wasn't a good businessman and you know, in this business they always tell you you have to make a name for yourself. Even now people…

473.t: Burke gets Capitol to raise his royalty from four to five percent; end of tape
473.s: After the Astaire show, Burke argued for a higher graduated royalty and won 5 percent; Jones, who never knew royalties escalate, was happy with a penny, and Dance ends the session to drive to Connecticut.
473.q: But a lot of things like that he did then. Another thing about Capitol, when we got out there and we started doing the Fred Astaire show, well the royalties was graduated up, you know, like --
